newsitem.title: CHINA: China weakens barrier between town and village.
newsitem.headline: China weakens barrier between town and village.

text.p: China has begun a major reform of its strict household regulation system that will weaken the administrative barrier between urban and rural residents, state media said on Thursday.

Under a reform plan proposed by the Public Security Bureau and approved by the State Council, or cabinet, former farmers who worked and lived in small cities or towns would be able to win official urban residency, the China news service said.
"China has implemented a major reform of the system of controlling registered permanent residence it has had for nearly half a century," the official agency said.
"From now on there will be a comparatively big increase in the figures for urban population in China's population statistics," it said.
China has long tried to control the movement of its population through a strict system of household registration that ties people to their native areas and divides them into rural or urban residents.

Household registration has a profound influence on individuals by defining many of their economic and social rights, obligations and opportunities, but the system has come under increasing pressure during nearly two decades of reform.
Tens of millions of rural residents have left their villages in search of work, forming a vast "floating population" that swirls around the edges of China's more prosperous cities.

Semi-private village and township enterprises had helped to soak up 100 million surplus rural labourers, but more than 100 million more were still in their villages -- and the number of surplus farmers was growing, the China news service said.

The expanding surplus rural workforce had already begun influencing village economic development and social stability, it quoted State Council Secretary-General Luo Gan as telling a national teleconference to push the new reforms.
"Reforming and improving the household registration management system of small towns and cities will help to ease the population pressure on medium and larger cities," Luo said.
Many sociologist and economists believe that the days of strict residency controls are numbered as China dismantles its strict communist social controls in favour of a market-driven economic system.

Lack of formal residency puts many economic migrants largely outside the legal system, causing widespread corruption and putting huge strain on government departments in charge of welfare, family planning, sanitation and law enforcement.

However, state leaders who prize stability above all else have been highly cautious about scrapping the decades-old system, and the China news service made clear that the effects of the new reforms would be carefully watched.
Earlier changes to the household registration system had caused problems such as the corrupt sale of residency permits, it said.

"Because of this, the State Council has strictly defined the limits on the implementation of this reform," it said. "Local government below the county level will have no right to determine or expand the scope of this reform experiment."
Only former farmers who had lived in pilot cities for at least two years would be eligible to become permanent residents, the Xinhua news agency said in a separate report.
